title: I am Joseph (Genesis 45:1–15)
hookLine: he weeps so loudly Egypt hears; "it was not you that sent me hither, but God"

lines: HE WEEPS SO LOUD EGYPT HEARS.
cards: Judah finishes speaking, and the room goes quiet. The governor can't hold it anymore. Everyone out! he shouts at his servants.
Clear the room! The Egyptian guards and attendants file out, and the door closes on eleven frightened Hebrew shepherds and one Egyptian lord. Then he starts crying.
Not quietly. He weeps so loudly that the Egyptians outside hear it, and word reaches Pharaoh's house. The brothers have no idea what's happening.
They think they're about to be enslaved.

teach.b: Then, in Hebrew, with no interpreter now: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" Ani Yosef.
The brothers can't answer; the text says they were terrified at his presence. The rabbis noticed that silence.
One old teacher said: if the brothers couldn't answer Joseph when he spoke one sentence, how will any of us answer on the day we're shown our whole lives? Joseph sees their fear.
Come near to me, please, he says, and they come near. I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. He says it.
He doesn't pretend it didn't happen. Then: don't be grieved, and don't be angry with yourselves. God sent me ahead of you to preserve life.
Two years of famine, five more to come, and I'm here to keep you alive.

teach.h: NOT YOU THAT SENT ME, BUT GOD.
teach.b: And the line the whole story has been building to: "So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God." What is Joseph doing? Readers honestly disagree.
Some hear real forgiveness: he's found meaning in his suffering, and he frees his brothers from its weight. Others notice he's reframing it for himself, that he needed this story to survive.

And the Torah doesn't say the brothers were off the hook; years later, they're still afraid of him. What the text does show is a man looking back over the pit, the slavery and the prison, and seeing a path.
Not a good thing. A road that led somewhere. Then he kisses all his brothers and weeps on them.

teach.h: AND AFTER THAT HIS BRETHREN TALKED WITH HIM.
teach.b: "And after that his brethren talked with him." For the first time since the coat.

how: Jewish tradition reads Joseph's words as a model of forgiveness that names the wrong honestly, and Jewish teachers also stress that forgiving does not require pretending a harm was good.

when Jacob dies, they're afraid he'll take revenge. the Torah doesn't tie it up neatly.

games.q: you're Joseph. your brothers are standing in front of you, terrified and silent, after you've told them who you are. what do you say next?
o: remind them exactly what they did.
leave them alone to think about it.
games.why: "come near to me, I pray you." then he names the sale, and tells them it was not you that sent me here, but God.

practice: Think of something hard that happened a while ago, not your deepest wound, something you've had time with, and ask one question: did it lead anywhere, to a strength, a friend, a path you wouldn't have found?
You don't have to say it was good, or that anyone was right to do it. Some hurts don't reframe, and that's allowed; just look for the road.

wordCard.voice: Ani Yosef, Hebrew for I am Joseph: two words that ended twenty-two years of silence, and the brothers finally see who has been standing in front of them.

orig.note: Hebrew: I am Joseph. Yosef means he will add.

carryVoice: Your line: it led somewhere. Joseph names the wrong, and still sees the road. Day seventy-four.
